newsitem.title: USA: U.S. welfare cuts to reduce food for poor - study.
newsitem.headline: U.S. welfare cuts to reduce food for poor - study.

text.p: The nation's largest food bank said Monday food stamp cuts contained in the welfare law passed last year would create an "unprecedented threat to the food security of poor Americans."

A study commissioned by Second Harvest estimated that food stamp cuts in the law would amount to $28 billion from 1997 to 2002, resulting in the withdrawal of nearly 24 billion pounds of food from the poor, or an average of 4 billion pounds a year.
Second Harvest, which distributed 1 billion pounds of food last year, commissioned the study from the Tufts University Centre on Hunger, Poverty and Nutrition Policy.
"This is an unprecedented threat to the food security of poor Americans," the center's director, Larry Brown, said.

Second Harvest president Christine Vladimiroff said donations of food to the charity from federal agencies had already declined nearly 11 percent from 1991 to 1995. Private donations leveled off last year.

"Some federal officials look to the private sector to make up for government retrenchments, but our resources were depleted even before passage of this law," Vladimiroff said. "There is no way we or even all private agencies combined can make up for the loss of 24 billion pounds over the next six years."
